middle_heading: Before you invest in your brand
middle_body: A strong name is only valuable if you can use it, protect it, and grow with it.\n\nTrademark planning helps founders avoid preventable rebrands, filing mistakes, and ownership problems before they become expensive.

Choosing and clearing a brand name

Understanding federal trademark filings

Identifying the right owner and filing strategy

Avoiding common mistakes that weaken protection

For founders, creators, consumer brands, software companies, and growing businesses preparing to launch or expand.\n\nUse the guide as a practical starting point before investing further in a name, product, or brand identity.
Lady Gaga’s trademarks span 65 records and 18 distinct marks. Her stage name is only the center of the map.

Her fan community became a brand asset. LITTLE MONSTERS earned four federal registrations in 2013 covering social networking, streaming, and online entertainment. Those registrations have since left the register, but the lesson stands: communities can be brand assets too.
Beauty is the busiest corner of Gaga's portfolio. Earlier fragrance filings like EAU DE GAGA, BAD ROMANCE, and LADY GAGA FAME mapped this ambition years earlier.

Brand architecture is important. Even Gaga's characters got filings. MISS ASIA KINNEY covered pet-care products and Gaga's male alter ego JO CALDERONE drew seven intent-to-use applications in a single day in 2011.
middle_subheading: From JO CALDERONE to MISS ASIA KINNEY

middle_body: Albums, tours, and even a song were filed. GRIGIO GIRLS was filed for wine and a GAGA registration for wines is still live today.

A valuable brand is rarely one name. Map your brand universe early. Your portfolio should include a protection strategy timeline that covers your core mark, products, community, personas, and campaigns.
This ratio shows what an actively managed trademark portfolio looks like.

middle_body: LADY GAGA was officially registered for entertainment services in 2009, then came clothing, followed by recordings. By 2017, one merchandise registration spanned 14 classes.

Each class is a separate scope of protection. Coverage is a choice you design, not something registration hands you automatically. These classes ranged from cosmetics, clothing, entertainment, streaming, jewelry, music, and even wine.
All four pending applications were filed on an intent-to-use basis, reserving priority before products ship. This includes HAUS LABS lines and LADY GAGA cosmetics-accessory filings.

middle_body: Portfolios get pruned as plans mature. HAUS BEAUTY and an early HAUS LABS application lapsed, but refiled versions registered in 2022 and 2025.

middle_body: The playbook in these records scales to any company: register the core early, add categories as commerce follows, use intent-to-use filings to hold the runway, and let filings that no longer serve the plan go.
Abandoned just means an application ended before registration.

middle_body: An intent-to-use filing can only be registered once real commercial use is proven. Plans often change before that point.
middle_subheading: Every abandoned application was filed based on intent-to-use

middle_body: The reasoning behind abandonment is often unclear, but it can occur if plans shift, a deadline passes, a statement of use is never filed, or a filing is replaced by a better one.
Sixteen HAUS OF GAGA applications filed in a single day in 2011 went abandoned. Years later, HAUS LABS registrations issued and are live.

BAD ROMANCE’s fragrance application is abandoned, but the name is not necessarily up for grabs. Common-law use, related live registrations, and other rights can survive an abandoned application. Availability takes a full search.
Abandonment is usually procedural. Don’t treat an abandoned application as clearance to adopt the name yourself.

Dead is a database label, not a single event. Of the 52 inactive records supplied, 42 are applications that never registered, and 10 are registrations that issued — and later left the register. The difference matters.

An application that ends before registration is abandoned. HAUS OF GAGA, JO CALDERONE, and GRIGIO GIRLS filings ended this way — intent-to-use claims that were never perfected, not registrations that were lost.

Registration is not permanent. LITTLE MONSTERS registered in 2013 for streaming and social networking and ARTPOP registered in 2015 for merchandise. Both left the register. Ongoing maintenance is required to keep registrations alive.

middle_heading: Gaga’s Rights May Survive,\nDead or Alive
middle_body: A single dead record tells you almost nothing until you read the portfolio around it. One HAUS LABORATORIES registration from 2015 is dead while another HAUS LABORATORIES registration from 2022 is live.
In a working portfolio, eras end and products relaunch. Campaign marks like THE ARTPOP BALL come and go while the core LADY GAGA registrations stay live.

Never treat a dead-record search as a clearance opinion. A dead federal record answers one narrow question. It cannot tell you whether use continues, common-law rights persist, or a related live filing exists.

middle_heading: Swift’s Name Is Just The Start
middle_body: U.S. trademark records for the Taylor Swift brands span 113 filings and registrations across 15 distinct marks. The catalog covers her name, initials, album eras, and lyrics.
Fifteen live T. S. registrations cover merchandise from jewelry to bed linens. TS and SWIFT add more. Even initials can anchor a product line.
TAYLOR SWIFT FEARLESS registrations cover guitars and backpacks. SPEAK NOW registrations cover jewelry, blankets, and retail services. Each era became its own product brand.
In one October 2014 weekend, lyric phrases were filed across dozens of merchandise categories. Catchphrases can be brand assets too.

middle_heading: Swift’s Marks Live In An LLC
middle_body: Every live registration lists TAS Rights Management, LLC as owner. Only the unfinished early filings still name Taylor Swift individually. Mature brands get a corporate home.
A brand universe includes the name, the shorthand, the product eras, and the catchphrases. Decide what you own, then protect the pieces that matter.
Every live registration in these records shows a Section 1(a) use basis. The register mirrors real commerce, not speculation.
TAYLOR SWIFT was registered for entertainment services in 2008 from a 2007 filing. Recordings, clothing, jewelry, and retail followed. Thirty-five name registrations remain live.
Filings cluster around album cycles, with coordinated waves across merchandise categories. The portfolio grows on the business calendar.
TAYLOR SWIFT anchors the portfolio. T. S. and SWIFT cover shorthand branding. FEARLESS and SPEAK NOW cover eras. Layered coverage closes gaps.
Seven SPEAK NOW registrations remain live while one for website services lapsed. Commercially relevant coverage stays. The rest can go.
Register the core name early, add layers around it, file in waves as the business grows, and keep only what commerce still supports.
The records include 36 abandoned applications, most from the famous 2014 lyric wave. Abandoned means one thing: the application ended before registration.
THIS SICK BEAT was filed in 16 categories. Thirteen applications went abandoned. Only three reached registration, each on a use basis.
An abandoned status never explains itself. A deadline passes, use is not proven, or plans change. The record shows the ending, not the reason.
34 of the 36 abandoned filings were intent-to-use reservations. LOVE LOVE LOVE was reserved in 2007 and again in 2010, and completed neither time.
An abandoned application does not clear the name for others. Related registrations, common-law use, and new filings can still block adoption.
Reserve names ahead of launch, calendar every deadline, and let go of filings the business outgrew. An abandoned application is a decision point, not a failure.
Dead covers two endings here: 36 applications that never registered, and 11 registrations that issued and later left the register. Same label, different stories.
Several 2014 lyric marks registered for tops and notebooks, then left the register within a few years. A registration is a maintenance commitment.

middle_body: SWIFTSTAKES, a sweepstakes brand, registered in 2015 and later left the register. Campaign brands can retire while the core portfolio stays intact.
No TAYLOR SWIFT registration in these records has died. The dead file holds experiments and era marks. Portfolios shed leaves, not trunks.
A dead record cannot tell you a name is free. Live related registrations, continued use, and refiled applications can still stand in the way.
Statuses are labels, not verdicts. Before relying on any dead record, read the family of filings around it and get a real clearance review.
Records for Little Miss Mogul, LLC, the company behind the Nicki Minaj brands, span 35 filings and registrations across 10 marks. The range runs from perfume to restaurants.
One November 2012 wave filed NICKI MINAJ across 20 categories: candles, candy, jewelry, restaurants, even soft drinks. Filing breadth is a snapshot of ambition.
Every live registration in the records is for fragrance and body care, including two NICKI MINAJ beauty registrations and PINK FRIDAY NICKI MINAJ perfume.
Fragrance names got their own filings. MINAJESTY registered in 2015. O ONIKA, ONIKA NICKI MINAJ, and TRINI GIRL were explored through applications that never finished.
PINK FRIDAY began as an album era and returned as a product line. Three 2024 intent-to-use applications cover nail products under the album name.
A brand universe can be wide or deep. File where the business is real, and let one strong lane carry the name further than twenty weak ones.

middle_heading: Minaj’s Live Marks Tell A Story
middle_body: The records hold 3 live registrations, 3 pending applications, and 29 records no longer active. What survived is exactly where the products shipped.
All three live registrations sit in one class: cosmetics and fragrance. PINK FRIDAY NICKI MINAJ perfume registered in 2014, and NICKI MINAJ beauty followed in 2015 and 2020.
The 2012 wave reserved NICKI MINAJ across 20 categories on an intent-to-use basis. None of those completed. Depth beat breadth.
Three PINK FRIDAY applications for nail products were filed before launch on an intent-to-use basis. Reserving priority ahead of a product drop is the playbook working.

middle_heading: Minaj Runs Marks Through An LLC
middle_body: Every record lists Little Miss Mogul, LLC, a Delaware company, as owner. Like other major artists, the brand lives in a dedicated entity.
Register where revenue is real, reserve names just ahead of launches, and let speculative coverage go. A narrow live portfolio beats a wide dead one.
The records include 27 abandoned applications. Every one was filed on an intent-to-use basis. Abandoned means the application ended before registration, nothing more.
The November 2012 filing spree reached from flatware to restaurants. All 20 applications went abandoned. Reservations lapse when plans stay plans.
Five fragrance-name applications were filed between 2014 and 2016 and none completed. Filing can be part of how a brand explores its options.

PRETTY GANG’s applications are abandoned, but that alone does not free the name. Live registrations, common-law use, and refilings can still block adoption.
File wide only when you mean to follow through, calendar every deadline, and treat any abandoned record as a question to investigate, not an answer.
Most dead records here are applications that never registered. Two are different: registrations that issued, lived for years, and then left the register.
MINAJESTY, a perfume brand, registered in 2015 and later left the register. A registration is a maintenance commitment, not a permanent asset.
One NICKI MINAJ cosmetics registration is dead. Two NICKI MINAJ beauty registrations are live. A dead record beside a living family means pruning, not retreat.
While old records died, new filings arrived. Three 2024 PINK FRIDAY applications for nail products show a portfolio that prunes and replants.
A dead record answers one narrow question. Continued use, live family registrations, and new applications can all still stand between you and a name.
Two dead registrations, twenty-seven dead applications, and a live beauty core tell one story: statuses are labels. Read the whole portfolio before relying on any one of them.
Records for BGK Trademark Holdings, LLC span 96 filings and registrations across 68 marks. The catalog covers the core name, a fan community, fragrances, charity, family names, and whole album eras.
The earliest registration in the records issued in 2004 and is still live, covering posters, clothing, and entertainment services. A 2012 fragrance registration joined it.
The fan community name BEYHIVE has held a live registration for web-based fan club services since 2012. Communities can be durable brand assets.
A fragrance dynasty runs through the records. Four HEAT-era registrations came and went while BEYONCÉ RISE and SHIMMERING HEAT remain live today.
Family names are portfolio assets too. BLUE IVY CARTER, SIR CARTER, and RUMI CARTER filings run through the records, refiled across a decade and pending today.
An empire is a portfolio with layers: name, community, products, causes, and eras. Protect the layers that last, and refile for the ones still coming.
The records split into 9 live registrations, 38 pending applications, and 49 inactive records. The pending pile is the tell: this portfolio is still expanding.
One April 2024 wave brought 21 filings: COWBOY CARTER, KNTRY RADIO, BUCKIN’, and more, each claiming merchandise classes while the era peaked.
BLUE IVY CARTER was filed in 2012, again in 2016, and again in 2023. The first two lapsed. The third is pending. Persistence is a strategy.
The era waves are intent-to-use filings across many classes, reserving priority before products exist. Coverage is claimed while attention peaks.
Every record lists BGK Trademark Holdings, LLC, a Delaware company. The pattern holds across major artists: valuable marks live in dedicated entities.
Register the core, keep the community and causes covered, file each era as it arrives, and refile what matters until it lands.
The records include 36 applications that ended before registration. Every one was an intent-to-use reservation. Abandoned describes the application, never the brand.
THANKYOULOVEBEYONCÉ and four sibling filings arrived together in May 2024 and all lapsed. Filing several variants is one way a name gets explored.
Two broad 2011 filings claimed the single letter B and B REVOLUTION across 14 classes each. Neither completed. Breadth without launch lapses.
THE MRS. CARTER SHOW, BLACKBIRD, and early BLUE IVY CARTER applications all ended without explanation on the record. Statuses show endings, not reasons.
An abandoned application does not free a name. Refilings in these very records prove the point: BLUE IVY CARTER lapsed twice and is pending again today.
Reserve boldly if you will follow through, calendar the deadlines, and read any abandoned record as an opening question. The owner may already be refiling.
Thirteen dead records here actually registered first: fragrances, personas, even phones. The other 36 never got that far. Dead is a category, not a cause.
HEAT KISSED, HEAT SEDUCTION, WILD ORCHID, and PULSE all registered and later left the register, while RISE and SHIMMERING HEAT remain live. Product lines rotate and portfolios rotate with them.
The alter ego held two registrations for clothing and recordings. Both later left the register. Personas can retire; the records simply mark the exit.
Three 2007-era filings for handheld devices, including BPHONE, registered and later died. Technology moves, and portfolios shed what the business outgrew.
A YONCÉ clothing registration died, and a fresh YONCÉ application arrived in 2025. A dead record is often a chapter break, not the end of the book.
Dead registrations, lapsed applications, live refilings: one name can hold all three at once. Statuses are labels. Clearance takes the whole record.
A clearance search reviews existing trademark records and marketplace uses that may conflict with a proposed mark. The question is similarity and relatedness, not just identical wording.
Marks conflict when they are confusingly similar and the goods are related. A changed letter or an added hyphen rarely helps when the marks still sound alike.
Goods can be legally related across different trademark classes: clothing and hats, banking and mortgage lending. Searching one class can miss the conflict that matters.
Rights can arise from marketplace use without any registration. State records, domains, social platforms, and app stores all belong in a comprehensive search.
A registered domain is not clearance. An approved LLC name is not clearance. Neither is a search that stops at one class or skips pending applications.
A search assesses risk. It cannot guarantee registration or silence every objection. Run it before domains, packaging, inventory, and advertising, while changing course is still cheap.
A trademark application makes factual representations about ownership, use, and the goods behind the mark. Five steps deserve attention before anything gets submitted.
The applicant should be whoever controls the goods sold under the mark: a person, an LLC, or a corporation. Naming the wrong owner can be impossible to fix after filing.
Check live registrations and pending applications for lookalikes and soundalikes, then search beyond the federal database. An available domain proves nothing about trademark rights.
A winery sells wine, not labels. List what the business genuinely offers or intends to offer. You can narrow an application later, but you cannot broaden it.
middle_subheading: Goods and services set the scope

middle_body: Already selling? File use-in-commerce under Section 1(a). Launching soon? Intent-to-use under Section 1(b) reserves priority, with proof of use and fees to follow.
middle_subheading: Use now, or intent to use

middle_body: Real marketplace evidence is required: labels, packaging, or a live sales page. Mockups get refused. Fees run per class and stay paid even if the application fails.
Strong protection starts before filing and continues long after. Five decisions determine whether a trademark becomes an asset or a liability.
Creamy for yogurt describes; it does not distinguish. Descriptive wording is hard to register and harder to enforce. Invented, arbitrary, and suggestive names protect better.
Buying the domain and designing packaging before searching creates avoidable risk. Conflicts come from sound, meaning, and impression, not just exact matches.
middle_subheading: Love the name after you search

middle_body: The application is a set of factual statements. Wrong owner, wrong goods, wrong basis, or a mockup specimen can narrow protection or sink the filing entirely.
Inconsistent spelling, generic use, and the registration symbol before registration all erode a brand. Pair the mark with the product name and license it with quality controls.
Registrations need maintenance filings between years five and six, then every decade. Miss one and the registration can die while the business is thriving.

Stagevest is a professional networking and collaboration platform built for the music industry. Artists, musicians, producers, and event organizers use it to connect, communicate, discover opportunities, and collaborate.
The registration became effective March 31, 2026, and was entered on the register on June 26, 2026.
Stagevest also secured a separate registration for its sound-wave logo. It covers the same core software, networking, and music-industry platform services.

A word mark protects the brand name itself. A figurative mark protects the visual design used to represent the brand. Registering both can create broader and more flexible protection as a company grows.
